The 2026 Georgia gubernatorial election will take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the governor of Georgia. Incumbent Republican governor Brian Kemp is ineligible to seek re-election to a third consecutive term.

Primary elections were held on May 19, 2026, with a primary runoff held on June 16. Businessman Rick Jackson and incumbent Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones received the most votes in the first round of the Republican primary, but failed to reach the 50% threshold, causing a runoff which Jackson won. Jackson's campaign was predominantly self-funded, managing to overcome an endorsement for Jones from President Donald Trump and Kemp. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Democratic nomination without a runoff against six other candidates.

The 2026 gubernatorial primary was the first time that Democratic turnout exceeded that of Republicans since 2006.

If Lance Bottoms is elected, she would be the first female and first African-American governor of Georgia and could be the first female African-American governor in United States history. If Jackson is elected, he would be the oldest elected governor of Georgia at the age of 72 surpassing Lamartine Griffin Hardman.

Background

[edit]

Georgia is considered a swing state at the federal level, but the state has maintained a Republican lean at the state level, with Republicans holding all statewide executive offices in the 2022 midterms, where incumbent governor Brian Kemp was re-elected in a rematch against Democrat Stacey Abrams by a 7.5 percent margin.[1] Republicans also control both the state senate and House of Representatives, together with Kemp's governorship establishing a government trifecta, alongside an all but one Republican pick on the state's supreme court. A year prior to the 2026 elections, the 2025 Georgia Public Service Commission special election resulted in two Democrats being elected to the Commission, both by landslide victories, and marking the first time that Democrats won any seats on the PSC since the 2000 elections or any state-wide non-federal offices since the 2006 elections.[2][3] Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Georgia since 1998.

Republican primary

[edit]

Candidates

[edit]

With Kemp term-limited, speculation mounted about Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones, Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, and Attorney General Chris Carr. Carr and Raffensperger sought to associate themselves with Kemp, drawing on his relative popularity.[4] Jones sought to ally himself with Trump, who endorsed him in August 2025.

Rick Jackson, a healthcare CEO, announced his campaign in February 2026. Previously unknown in the political realm, Jackson quickly consolidated support from right-wing primary voters, in part due to his significant personal financial resources. Jackson spent more than $83 million in personal funds during the primary. Jackson's campaign emphasized his success as a self-made billionaire, highlighting his impoverished childhood. Jackson also sought to tie himself to Trump, claiming he would be "Trump's favorite governor" and "just like Trump, but with a Southern tone."[5] An aggressive television ad campaign allowed Jackson to take a small polling lead by spring 2026. Jackson's self-funding represented the largest amount any candidate had ever spent in a primary race for Georgia governor.[5]

Jones's campaign focused primarily on rural connections, Trump, and support from Republican allies in the General Assembly. Jones accused Jackson of "made his fortune recruiting for Planned Parenthood" and funding Transgender surgery for minors.[6] Jackson denied these accusations and filed for defamation against Jones, a lawsuit he later dropped.[7]

Results

[edit]

Jackson won the runoff by a 5-point margin, despite Kemp endorsing Jones two days before the vote. With the Democratic primary already over, focus shifted to the candidates' ability to counter Keisha Lance Bottoms. Jackson had consistently attacked Bottoms's record as mayor since he launched his campaign.

In the previous two occasions (2018 and 2010) where the Republican primary did not feature an incumbent governor, the plurality-winner in the primary went on to lose the primary runoff. This trend repeated itself in 2026.
